subject: dark gas planet
title: There's a Planet Darker Than Coal, and Nobody Knows Why

scenes.text: There's a planet darker than coal, and nobody knows why.
It's a gas giant the size of Jupiter, 750 light-years away. Astronomers call it Tres 2 b.
It reflects less than one percent of the light that hits it. Black acrylic paint reflects more.
Jupiter bounces back more than a third of its sunlight, thanks to bright clouds. This world is too hot for those: over 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit.
Something in its air swallows the light. Scientists have suggested sodium, potassium or titanium oxide. None of them fully explains it.
All it gives off is a faint red glow, in the dark.

description:
There is a planet darker than coal, and nobody is sure why.
TrES-2b is a Jupiter-sized gas giant about 750 light-years away in the constellation Draco. Using NASA's Kepler space telescope, David Kipping and David Spiegel measured how much starlight it reflects: less than one percent, which makes it blacker than coal, less reflective than black acrylic paint and darker than any planet or moon in our solar system (Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 2011). Jupiter, by comparison, reflects more than a third of the sunlight that reaches it because of its bright clouds. TrES-2b orbits only about three million miles from its star and is heated to more than 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit (980 Celsius), too hot for such clouds. Light-absorbing vaporised sodium and potassium or gaseous titanium oxide have been proposed, but none fully accounts for the darkness. The planet is so hot that it gives off a faint red glow.
What do you think is hiding in its air? Comment below.
first_comment: One of its discoverers said the cause may be a chemical nobody has thought of yet. What's your guess?
